title: The Longest Tube
principle: Digestion is taking food apart into pieces small enough to cross the wall.

t: There is a tube running right through you, about nine metres long. What is inside it is not inside you.
A nine-metre tube runs through you from end to end. Everything in it is topologically outside your body — you are a very elaborate doughnut.
sub: Nothing counts as being in you until it crosses the wall.
Nothing has entered you until it crosses the gut wall, which is where the interesting part happens.

t: Digestion is taking food apart into pieces small enough to cross the wall.
Digestion is controlled disassembly: polymers broken back down into the monomers they were built from.
Hydrolysis of polymers into monomers — starch to glucose, protein to amino acids, fat to fatty acids — which are then small enough to be absorbed and generic enough to rebuild anything.
The elegance is that the monomer set is universal, so an organism can dismantle any other organism and reuse the parts. Digestion is not purification; it is reduction to a common currency.
sub: Then you build your own things out of the pieces.
You do not absorb a cow's proteins — you absorb amino acids and build your own out of them.
This is also why food allergy exists: an intact protein that slips across the wall is exactly the thing the immune system is built to notice.

And why insulin has to be injected rather than swallowed. It is a protein, and the gut would take it apart into amino acids before it could do anything — the delivery problem, not the chemistry, is what kept it a needle for a century.

q: What is absorbed across the gut wall?
What is the absorbed form, and why that form?
options: Small pieces: sugars, amino acids, fatty acids
The food itself, in small lumps
why: Big things cannot cross the wall, and anyway they are built to somebody else's plan. You take them apart into the standard pieces and build your own.
Monomers cross, polymers do not. That solves two problems at once — size, which the membrane lesson covered, and specification, since a cow's protein is the wrong protein for you regardless.

Reduction to monomers is what makes any food substitutable for any other. It is also why the process must be thorough: an intact protein crossing the barrier is precisely the signal the immune system treats as foreign, which is the basis of food allergy.

t: Your small intestine is folded so much that it has the surface area of a tennis court.

Absorption rate depends on surface area, so the small intestine is folded, and the folds carry villi, and the villi carry microvilli. Three levels of folding turn a few metres of tube into around 30 square metres — the same optimisation, on the same variable, as the lungs. When that surface is damaged, as in coeliac disease, the problem is not the tube but the area.
